questions.prompt: There are {rows} rows and {count:company} different values in {role:company}. Is each row one person or one company?
questions.why: Counts, duplicates and who to call all depend on whether a row is a person or a company.

fact.statement: One row in this list is, per the owner: {answer_labels}.

questions.prompt: {role:email} has {count:email} different addresses on {rows:email} rows. When two rows share the same {role:email}, should they count as one person?
questions.recommend_basis: Some addresses repeat ({count:email} different addresses on {rows:email} rows), and shared inboxes such as info@ addresses are common enough to check first.
questions.why: Duplicates inflate counts and lead to the same person being called twice.

fact.statement: Rows that share the same {role:email}, per the owner: {answer_labels}.

questions.prompt: What do the {count:lifecycle_stage} stages in {role:lifecycle_stage}, such as {values:lifecycle_stage}, mean here?
questions.why: Stage names look standard, but each team uses them differently, and the funnel is only right with your meanings.

questions.prompt: {role:lead_status} uses {count:lead_status} short codes such as {values:lead_status}. What do they stand for?

options.label: Another tab explains them
options.desc: A tab or file; name it

questions.why: Qualified is your team's call, and the call list ranks on it.

fact.statement: A good-fit contact is judged by, per the owner: {answer_labels}.

questions.why: It separates live contacts from dead ones in every count.

outputs.title: Call list
outputs.pitch: Call list: contacts ranked by fit and recent activity, duplicates merged and opt-outs removed, saved as a new file.

outputs.title: List health check
outputs.pitch: List health check: duplicate people, blank fields, cold contacts and missing owners, counted field by field.

outputs.title: Segment map
outputs.pitch: Segment map: contacts grouped by source, stage and industry, with counts and how complete each group is.

outputs.title: Contacts to revenue
outputs.pitch: Contacts to revenue: connect a deals or orders file on email or company and see which contacts became customers, by source.

outputs.title: Guide for the next owner
outputs.pitch: Guide for the next owner: a plain page on where this list came from, what each stage and status means, who may be emailed and how to keep it clean.

outputs.title: App blueprint
outputs.pitch: App blueprint: a light CRM that takes new contacts from forms and imports, merges duplicates, scores fit and assigns an owner.

gotchas.say: {role:postal} may have lost leading zeros in Excel, so a code like 02134 can show as 2134.
{role:notes} holds remarks about people. Those stay on this machine and never go into the file.
{role:lifecycle_stage} shows where each contact is today; one export has no record of how they moved between stages.
{role:email} is blank on some rows, so those contacts cannot be matched to other files by email.
{role:opt_out} records who asked not to be contacted, and any list pulled from this file leaves those people out.
{role:owner} is blank on some rows, so those contacts belong to no one.
{role:lead_source} mixes values such as {values:lead_source}; the same source spelled two ways splits the counts.
Titles and work emails go out of date as people change jobs; measured B2B contact data decays about 12% a year.
Phone numbers in {role:phone} can be written many ways, so one number can look like two until formats are cleaned.
Company names vary (Acme Inc, ACME, Acme Incorporated), so counts by {role:company} can split one company into several.

graph.sentence: Dots are companies, sources, owners and stages. People appear when records are turned on. Lines show who works where and where they came from.

rules.basis: Measured B2B contact data decays about 12% a year, so titles and emails older than a year may be out of date.
